title: I Offer Events Neither Praise nor Blame
intro: The commentary Mu'jiz Ahmad relates that al-Mutanabbi's maternal grandmother wrote from Kufa to complain of his long absence. He answered from Baghdad asking her to join him. In that account she kissed the letter and died of a fever before they could meet. He imagines the ink on her teeth, weighs what his travels cost them both, and turns from a fever beyond the reach of his sword to enemies he can still face.

translation: I offer events neither praise nor blame.
Their blows are no folly, their restraint no forbearance.
1.sharh: He begins by withholding judgement from events. To call a blow foolish or restraint merciful is to imagine a mind behind it. His grief will shortly give that distinction a personal cost.

translation: A young man returns to what he was.
As he began, he returns. As he grew, he dwindles.
2.sharh: The two uncommon verbs at the end make a matched pair, to diminish and to increase. The line traverses a whole life in the opposite direction to its growth.

translation: God be with you, bereaved of the one you loved,
killed by a longing that brings you no shame.
3.sharh: For a moment it is the dead woman who is bereaved. Her absent grandson had seemed lost to her, and death from longing takes on a different sense when the loved one is her child.

translation: I long for the cup from which she drank.
For her resting place I love the earth and all it holds.
4.sharh: Sharing a cup would once have meant keeping her company. Death has become that cup, and grief makes even the earth that took her dear to him.

translation: I wept for her in fear while she lived.
Each of us long ago tasted the other's loss.
5.sharh: They mourned each other in advance. The word for bereavement often belongs to a parent who loses a child. He gives it to them both.

translation: Had separation killed everyone who loved,
a town she parted from for good would now be gone.
6.sharh: Her town still stands although she has broken with it for ever. By letting the town itself love her, he measures one woman's lethal longing against the grief of a whole community.

translation: I knew the nights before what they did to us.
When they struck me, I knew them no better.
7.sharh: He had known the power of time to separate people as a fact about other lives. It is the pronoun “us” that makes this stroke different.

translation: The nights gain by spoiling what profits another.
They eat and drink their fill when you hunger and thirst.
8.sharh: Al-Wahidi takes the nights as the subject. They feed on human deprivation. Ibn Furja hears a portrait of the grandmother here, finding sustenance in going hungry so that others can eat.

translation: My letter reached her after despair and sorrow.
She died of joy in me, and I of grief for her.
9.sharh: The same verb carries two very different deaths. The little pair “in me” and “for her” sends the force of the letter back to its writer.

translation: Joy is forbidden to my heart.
What killed her I count as poison now she is gone.
10.sharh: The poison is joy itself. A feeling he had hoped to give her can now never be harmless to him again.

translation: She marvels at my words and my handwriting, as though
among the letters she sees white-marked ravens.
11.sharh: He changes to the present tense and puts the reader beside her. A raven with a patch of white was proverbial for rarity. Dark ink against the pale page gives that rarity a visible form.

translation: She kisses it until its ink has turned
the rims of her eyes and her teeth black.
12.sharh: The ink travels from his hand to her face. The marks round the eyes suggest where else she has pressed the page while kissing it.

translation: Her flowing tears ceased, her eyelids dried,
and my love left her heart after drawing blood.
13.sharh: He lets dry eyes briefly suggest relief. Only death has stopped the tears, and he imagines the feeling they once carried as a wound inside the heart.

translation: Only death consoled her for my absence.
What cured her sickness was worse than the sickness.
14.sharh: The supposed cure is the bereavement he has just described. The line turns a conventional consolation for the end of suffering back on the people who offer it.

translation: I sought good fortune for her. I lost them both.
She was content with me, had I been content with her.
15.sharh: The two losses share a verb. He had thought the journey a service to her, only to realise that his presence was precisely the share of fortune she wanted.

translation: Now I ask the clouds for rain upon her grave.
Once I asked battle and solid spears to give me drink.
16.sharh: Asking rain for a grave is a prayer for the dead. When he once made the same request of a battlefield, the liquid he could expect from the spears was blood.

translation: Before her death I thought distance a great affliction.
What once was greatest has become the least.
17.sharh: Distance once had no rival as the worst thing that could happen. It has changed rank because it used to leave open the possibility of going home.

translation: Suppose I won redress for you against an enemy.
How could I win it for you against a fever?
18.sharh: A feud would give him an identifiable adversary and a recognised course of action. Repeating the same words with “fever” in the enemy's place exposes the limit of that power.

translation: The world did not close in on me for lack of space.
An eye that cannot see you is blind.
19.sharh: Space is still there in abundance. The trouble is what can be seen in it. One missing face cancels the use of his sight.

translation: My grief is that I cannot bend to kiss
your head and breast, both filled with sound judgement,
20.sharh: He longs to touch the head and breast where he locates her intelligence and judgement. The rare dual form behind “both” keeps the two parts of the body together.

translation: or meet your fragrant spirit,
as if the finest musk had once been its body.
21.sharh: The Arabic adjective can describe goodness and a pleasing scent. He turns that overlap into a whole body made of musk for the spirit to inhabit.

translation: Even were you not the noblest father's daughter,
being my mother would be illustrious ancestry enough.
22.sharh: Calling his grandmother his mother brings her one generation closer. She has just been honoured for her father. Now he claims a descendant can confer as much honour as an ancestor.

translation: If those who gloat enjoyed the day she died,
she bore in me the one to rub their noses in dust.
23.sharh: The Arabic puts the humiliation itself where a child would stand after “she bore”. Her surviving grandson makes their pleasure at her death short-lived.

translation: He left home holding no one higher than himself,
accepting judgement only from his Creator,
24.sharh: The “he” is the grandson she bore. He lets the imagined audience look at him from outside, as a man whose departure cost him dearly and whose independence he will still defend.

translation: taking no road but the heart of a dust cloud,
finding no flavour except in a noble deed.
25.sharh: Dust marks the thick of an encounter. The second image moves from the road under his feet to the taste in his mouth, a private sense of what makes the risk worthwhile.

translation: In every town they ask me what I am,
what I seek. What I seek is too great to name.
26.sharh: He borrows the wording of the question for his reply and withholds the name of his ambition. The enemies' children in the next line suggest why anyone would fear the answer.

translation: As though their sons already knew
I bring them orphanhood from its very source.
27.sharh: He speaks like someone bringing goods from the place that produces them. His commodity is fatherlessness, and its source is the killing of those children's fathers.

translation: To hold fire and water together in my hand
is no harder than to unite good fortune and understanding.
28.sharh: The short word jadd here means a person's luck. A man may judge well and still fail utterly in what he meant to achieve for someone he loves.

translation: Still I shall seek victory with its edge
and use it to take by force whatever comes.
29.sharh: “Its” has no named antecedent. The listener has to supply the sword from its cutting edge. It is the answer he imagines giving to fortune's refusal to help.

translation: I shall make it my greeting on the day we meet,
or forfeit my claim to be a lord and champion.
30.sharh: A greeting normally acknowledges a bond between two people. Here its entire content is the sword, and the titles he gives himself depend on his keeping that appointment.

translation: If fear of distance blunts my resolve for a goal,
nothing is further than the possible left unattempted.
31.sharh: The verb for blunting can be used of a sword. What goes blunt here is the will, and that can put an ordinary possibility further away than any distant goal.

translation: I belong to a people whose souls seem
too proud to dwell in flesh and bone.
32.sharh: His people court danger so readily that their souls seem impatient of their material lodging. The recording speaks of “their souls”, keeping the people for a moment in the third person.

translation: That is how I am, world. Go if you wish.
My soul, press further into what the world dreads.
33.sharh: Two direct addresses replace the earlier questions from strangers. He dismisses the world, then summons his own soul in the opposite direction, further into difficulty.

translation: May no hour pass over me that brings me no honour.
May no soul that submits to injustice keep me company.
34.sharh: He treats each hour, and even his own life, as company he might decline. The elegy ends with the conditions on which the survivor is willing to go on living.

1.1.3.head: أَرى
1.1.3.meaning: I show or offer. Events receive whatever praise or blame the speaker might express.

1.1.5.head: مَدح
1.1.5.meaning: Praise. Al-Nahari gives madh. The commentaries read hamd, praise or thanks for what events bring.

1.2.2.head: بَطش
1.2.2.meaning: A violent laying hold. The word gives events a hand that can strike or hold back.

1.2.6.head: حِلم
1.2.6.meaning: Forbearance, the self-restraint of someone who has power to punish.

2.1.6.head: مَرجِع
2.1.6.meaning: The point of return, here the state preceding life.

2.2.3.head: أُبدِيَ
2.2.3.meaning: Was first brought into being. The final glottal stop of the usual verb is softened.

2.2.4.head: أَكرى
2.2.4.meaning: Diminishes here, after the previous increase.

2.2.6.meaning: Grew or increased. It balances the preceding verb for dwindling.

3.1.1-2.head: لَكِ اللَّه
3.1.1-2.meaning: “God be yours”, a prayer for divine care addressed to the dead woman.

3.1.4.head: مَفجوعَة
3.1.4.meaning: Stricken by loss. The long absence has already felt to her like bereavement.

3.2.5.head: وَصم
3.2.5.meaning: A blemish on someone's good name.

4.1.3.head: الكَأس
4.1.3.meaning: A filled cup. To drink from this particular cup is to die.

4.2.2.head: مَثوى
4.2.2.meaning: A dwelling or the act of dwelling. Her resting there makes the earth dear.

5.1.3.head: خيفَة
5.1.3.meaning: Dread of something still to come.

5.2.3.head: ثُكل
5.2.3.meaning: Bereavement, especially a parent's loss of a child.

5.2.5.head: قِدماً
5.2.5.meaning: Long ago, well before news of her death.

6.2.4-6.head: أَجَدَّ صَرماً
6.2.4-6.meaning: “Made a fresh breach with it”, the separation her death imposes on her town.

7.1.2.meaning: The nights, a way of naming time by its succession of losses and changes.

8.1.1.head: مَنافِع
8.1.1.meaning: What benefits her or them. A feminine singular pronoun can point to the grandmother or back to the plural “nights”.

8.2.6.head: ظَمِئَ
8.2.6.meaning: Grow thirsty. The regular final glottal stop is softened at the rhyme.

9.1.5.head: تَرحَة
9.1.5.meaning: Grief or despondency, overturned by the arrival of the letter.

9.2.4-6.head: ماتَ غَمّاً
9.2.4-6.meaning: “I died of grief for her”, an answering death in a different sense.

10.2.6.head: سُمّ
10.2.6.meaning: Poison, how he now thinks of the joy that killed her.

11.1.2-4.head: لَفظ وخَطّ
11.1.2-4.meaning: His wording and his handwriting. The order is reversed in the diwan commentaries, which continue “as though she”.

11.2.4-5.head: غُراب أَعصَم
11.2.4-5.meaning: White-marked ravens. Such a bird was proverbial for something extraordinarily rare.

12.1.1.head: لَثِمَ
12.1.1.meaning: Kisses it, putting her mouth to the letter itself.

12.1.4.head: مِداد
12.1.4.meaning: Writing ink, still imagined as capable of leaving marks on the face.

12.2.1.head: مَحجِر
12.2.1.meaning: The sockets or rims of the eyes.

12.2.4.head: أَسحَم
12.2.4.meaning: Blackened, dark in colour. The plural covers the eye sockets and teeth alike.

13.1.1.meaning: Ceased to flow. An older verb used of both tears and blood.

13.2.6.meaning: Drew blood, the mark love leaves on her heart.

14.1.2.head: أَسلى
14.1.2.meaning: Console her or bring her forgetfulness of someone she misses.

14.2.3.head: السُّقم
14.2.3.meaning: Sickness, here the suffering of her long separation.

15.1.3.head: حَظّ
15.1.3.meaning: A share of worldly fortune, what he went away to seek for her.

15.2.7.head: قِسم
15.2.7.meaning: An allotted share, the amount of good fortune one will settle for.

16.1.2.head: اِستَسقى
16.1.2.meaning: Ask for water. A traditional blessing asks the clouds to rain upon a grave.

16.2.4.meaning: The clamour of battle, hence battle itself.

16.2.5-6.head: القَنا الصُّمّ
16.2.5-6.meaning: Solid, strong spear shafts. What they once yielded him was blood.

17.1.5.meaning: Distance from home or from those one loves.

18.1.1.head: هَب
18.1.1.meaning: Suppose me to have done this. The imperative asks her to entertain a possibility.

18.1.3.head: الثّار
18.1.3.meaning: Blood vengeance. The recitation smooths the glottal stop of tha'r into a long vowel.

18.1.6.meaning: Enemies or foes, a collective plural.

19.2.2.head: طَرف
19.2.2.meaning: An eye, or its power of sight.

20.1.5.head: أَكَبَّ
20.1.5.meaning: Bend over something, here to kiss her.

20.2.3.meaning: A shortened dual relative, “the two which”. The verb that follows also applies to both head and breast.

21.2.2-3.head: ذَكِيُّ المِسك
21.2.2-3.meaning: The most fragrant musk, powerful and penetrating.

22.2.3.head: الضَّخم
22.2.3.meaning: Illustrious in ancestry or standing, an epithet for the father.

23.1.5.head: يَومُها
23.1.5.meaning: Her day, the day she died. Another transmitted reading says “at her death”.

23.2.4-5.head: رَغم الأَنف
23.2.4-5.meaning: “Dust for their noses”, humiliation figured as forcing someone's nose to the earth.

24.1.1.meaning: Went into exile or lived away from home. The grandson speaks of himself in the third person.

24.2.5.head: حُكم
24.2.5.meaning: A ruling or authority that can bind him.

25.1.4-5.head: فُؤاد عَجاجَة
25.1.4-5.meaning: “The heart of a dust cloud”, the thick of battle.

25.2.4.head: مَكرُمَة
25.2.4.meaning: A noble deed by which someone earns honour.

26.2.5-7.head: جَلَّ أَن يُسَمّى
26.2.5-7.meaning: “Too great to be named”, a refusal that leaves his hearers to guess what he wants.

27.2.1.head: جَلوب
27.2.1.meaning: One who brings something in quantity, as a merchant might import goods.

27.2.4.head: مَعدِن
27.2.4.meaning: Places of origin or mines. Children become fatherless where their fathers are killed.

28.2.5.head: الجَدّ
28.2.5.meaning: Good fortune or luck. The vowel distinguishes it from jidd, earnest effort.

29.1.3.head: ذُباب السَّيف
29.1.3.meaning: The point or cutting edge of a sword. The weapon itself has yet to be named.

30.1.4.head: تَحِيَّة
30.1.4.meaning: A greeting at a meeting. His adversary is to receive a sword stroke.

30.2.5.head: القَرم
30.2.5.meaning: A leader above his peers, originally an outstanding breeding camel.

31.1.2.meaning: Blunted or chipped an edge, here taking the edge off resolve.

31.1.5.head: مَدى
31.1.5.meaning: The furthest point one aims to reach.

32.1.5.head: نَفس
32.1.5.meaning: Their souls. The commentaries read “our souls”, bringing the speaker inside the group he has named.

32.2.2.head: أَنَف
32.2.2.meaning: Proud disdain at being confined to something one regards as beneath oneself.

33.2.5.head: كَريهَة
33.2.5.meaning: Hardships or ordeals, especially encounters others shrink from.

33.2.6.head: قُدُماً
33.2.6.meaning: Forward, with determination. Earlier qidaman meant “long ago”.

34.1.6.head: أَعَزَّ
34.1.6.meaning: Bring me honour or preserve me from humiliation.

34.2.3.head: مُهجَة
34.2.3.meaning: The life-blood or soul, imagined here as a companion.
